parts.t: The Complete Guide

blocks.text: Buying a Chicken Farm in BC: Quota, Costs and BCCMB Transfers

parts.t: Buying a chicken farm in British Columbia is not like buying any other property. The land and the house are the easy part. The value, and the complexity, sits in the quota, the barns and an approval process most realtors have never taken a deal through. This guide covers how the system works, what farms actually cost, and how a purchase gets done.
On This Page
How quota works · Ways into the industry · The transfer process · What a chicken farm costs · Barn specs that matter · ALR rules · Common questions

blocks.text: How Chicken Quota Works in BC

parts.t: BC chicken production runs on supply management. To grow chicken commercially, you must hold quota registered with the BC Chicken Marketing Board, the provincial body that licenses growers, sets minimum live pricing and controls how much chicken gets produced. Quota is measured in production capacity and it is the single most valuable asset on most poultry farms, often worth more than the land under it.

Supply management is why operating chicken farms are stable businesses: growers receive a set minimum price per bird designed to cover production costs plus a return. It is also why you cannot simply buy an acreage, build a barn and start producing. No quota, no commercial production.
Note that quota systems are separate by sector. Broiler chicken,
turkey
table eggs
and broiler hatching eggs each have their own marketing board, their own quota and their own transfer rules. This guide focuses on broiler chicken, but the structure is similar across sectors.
Buy a complete operating farm

The most common route. A licensed grower sells the land, home, barns, equipment and quota as a going concern. You take over an operation that is already producing, often with grower relationships and processor arrangements in place. Browse current
chicken farms for sale in BC
to see what complete operations look like.
Buy quota separately and place it on an approved site

You can purchase quota from an existing grower and move it to a property you own, but the receiving site must be inspected and approved by the Board before birds are placed. This route suits existing growers expanding, or buyers who already own suitable ALR land with barns or room to build them.
The new entrant program, currently closed

The Board has historically run new entrant grower draws that allocated starter quota. It is not currently accepting applications or conducting draws in any region, though a New Entrant Grower consultation is underway that may reshape the program. Until anything changes, buying an existing farm or existing quota is effectively the only way in, which is a major reason operating farms hold their value so well.

Quota never transfers automatically with a property sale. When you buy a farm, the seller applies to the Board for approval of the quota transfer, and the Board reviews the buyer, the site and the transaction before production rights change hands. A share sale of a company that holds quota is still treated as a quota transaction, so structuring the deal through a corporation does not skip the process.

In practice, this means your purchase contract needs to be written around the approval: subject conditions tied to Board consent, a realistic completion timeline, and clarity on who bears the risk if approval is delayed. Deals go sideways when the contract treats a chicken farm like a house with a big shed. I write these offers so the quota, the equipment, the flock timing and the approvals are all accounted for from the first draft.

Timing matters more than most buyers expect. Farms change hands around flock cycles, and boards meet on a schedule, not on your closing date. Build the production calendar into the deal, not around it.

blocks.text: What a Chicken Farm Actually Costs

parts.t: Operating Fraser Valley poultry farms generally trade in the multi-million dollar range, but the total is really four assets priced together. Understanding each piece is how you avoid overpaying, and how sellers avoid leaving money on the table.
Quota
Priced per unit of production capacity, and often the largest line item. Value tracks industry pricing and scarcity, and the current new entrant freeze supports it.
Barns and Equipment
Modern tunnel-ventilated barns with automated systems command a premium. Older barns are priced against the cost to modernize them.
Land
ALR acreage values vary sharply by community. Farms in
Abbotsford
and
Chilliwack
price differently than
Langley
, where land carries a premium.
Residence
Most farms include a family home, sometimes two. The housing component is valued like any rural residential property and matters for financing.

Lenders familiar with supply-managed agriculture, including farm-specialized lenders, will finance quota as part of the operation. Expect them to scrutinize barn condition, production history and the quota transfer approval just as closely as the Board does.

blocks.text: Barn Specs That Move the Price

parts.t: Tunnel Ventilation and Cool Pads
End-to-end airflow with evaporative cooling pads. The modern standard for bird performance in summer heat, and a major value line versus older cross-ventilated barns.
Barn Computers
Automated controllers managing temperature, ventilation, feed and alarms. Newer control systems signal a barn that has been kept current.
Automated Feed and Water Lines
Pan feeding systems and nipple drinkers with scales that track bird weights. Labour efficiency is priced into the farm.
Backup Power and Alarms
A generator and alarm system is not optional on a modern poultry farm. Its absence is a diligence flag and a negotiating point.
Double-Decker Barns
Two-storey production barns that double capacity on a small footprint, common on tighter Fraser Valley acreages.
Manure Storage
Covered storage sized to the operation, required for environmental compliance and expected by every serious buyer.

Nearly every poultry farm in the region sits in the Agricultural Land Reserve. ALR rules generally allow barns, agricultural outbuildings, a principal residence and, with restrictions, additional dwellings, but the details vary by municipality. Water supply, natural gas service, setbacks from neighbouring properties and biosecurity separation from other poultry operations all affect whether a site can support expansion or a second barn. These are exactly the questions to answer before you write an offer, not after.

Two compliance items apply to every poultry property in BC regardless of size: mandatory biosecurity standards cover the entire industry, and any parcel where poultry is kept must be registered with the BC Premises Identification program so flocks can be traced during disease events like avian influenza. Given the Fraser Valley's history with avian flu, a farm's biosecurity setup, from controlled access points to barn entry protocols, is part of my diligence checklist on every poultry transaction.
Can I raise chickens without quota?

Yes, in small numbers. BC allows up to 200 birds per year for personal use without a permit. Between 200 and 2,000 birds per year, you need a Small Lot Permit from the Board: an annual application, a $20 fee, one permit per site, registration with the BC Premises ID program, and yearly placement and processing reports. All meat sold must be processed at a provincially or federally inspected facility, and municipal bylaws on keeping animals still apply. On the egg side, backyard flocks of up to 99 hens need no quota or registration at all. Anything beyond these thresholds requires quota. This is a popular angle for hobby farm buyers who want farm income without entering supply management.
How much does chicken quota cost?

There is no public price list. Quota trades privately between growers, values shift with industry pricing and scarcity, and the number you hear at the coffee shop is usually a year out of date. The honest answer is that quota is worth what a complete, approvable transaction says it is worth, which is why recent comparable farm sales, not rumours, are the basis I use for valuations on both sides of a deal.
Do turkey and egg farms work the same way?

Broadly yes, with their own boards and rules. One notable difference on the egg side: layer quota can also be acquired through quota exchanges the egg board runs several times a year, alongside private sales. See my pages on
turkey farms for sale in BC
and
egg and layer farms
for the sector-specific picture.
Where are most farms located?
The vast majority of BC poultry production sits in the Fraser Valley, with Abbotsford and Chilliwack holding the bulk of operations and additional farms through Langley and Mission. Start with all
poultry farms for sale in BC
for the full regional picture.
Where do I find the official rules?
The
BC Chicken Marketing Board
publishes grower licensing requirements and the current status of the new entrant program.

How-To Guide · British Columbia
Quota, BCCMB transfers
& barn values — explained.

Buying a supply-managed chicken farm is a different process from a typical real estate purchase. This guide covers how quota works, what the Board requires, and how to value the barns — the three things that decide the deal.
6 Questions Answered · Updated 2026
Understanding Quota
What exactly is chicken quota?
Quota is the licensed right to produce a set amount of meat chicken under BC’s supply-management system, administered by the
BC Chicken Marketing Board
. It’s a distinct, valuable asset — often the single largest component of a farm’s price — and it’s regulated separately from the land and buildings.
How does a BCCMB quota transfer actually work?

Both the seller and buyer apply to the Board. The Board reviews eligibility and premises, and — once conditions are met — typically cancels the seller’s quota and allots quota to the buyer. Quota can move with the registered premises or, in some cases, separately from the land. Every path requires Board approval. Quota does not simply run with the land. Any transfer must be applied for by both parties and approved by the applicable marketing board, and it isn’t included in a sale unless expressly stated in the Contract of Purchase and Sale.
Barns & Premises
Why do the barns matter so much?
Because the Board generally allots transferred quota only where there’s a
Board-approved building with adequate premises

for production. That means barn size, condition, ventilation, and approval status can determine whether a transfer can proceed — and future-expansion capacity is a critical consideration when evaluating any site.
What environmental rules apply to a chicken farm?

Provincial rules require poultry operations to manage manure, runoff, and impacts on nearby watercourses. Before buying, confirm the farm’s environmental compliance, manure-handling setup, and drainage — these affect both operating cost and risk.
Making the Purchase
How should quota be handled in the Contract of Purchase and Sale?

Spell it out. State the quota amount, class, and terms of transfer, and make clear that any transfer is subject to the applicable board’s approval and isn’t guaranteed simply by transferring title. No poultry quota is included unless the contract expressly says so — this protects both sides.
